extracted.intended_audience: artists, art-students, and art-critics (especially those concerned with landscape painting)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative criteria for judging or producing truthful landscape painting (clouds, earth, water, vegetation, foreground, distance, finish), as argued by John Ruskin. Emphasizes technical observation, demonstrable truth, and critic qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion as criterion only after long time
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion is no criterion of excellence, except after long periods of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reputation established by popular admiration is only trustworthy when it has been stable through long periods; transient majority approval does not determine real excellence. (Sec. 1)

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability and consistency of judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Right judgments are stable and consistent; erroneous opinions are transitory and inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because inconsistent erroneous opinions cannot maintain long-term authority, true excellence gradually communicates itself from competent minds to the wider public. Public applause that lacks consistency is not a reliable guide. (Sec. 1)

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence of the judge (equals or superiors required)
rubrics_metrics.description: A work can only be truly appreciated by judges who are its equal or superior in knowledge/skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inferior judges may enthusiastically mis-evaluate or fail to perceive high merit; proper comparison requires education and technical knowledge. Critics and students must be qualified to form grounded estimates. (Sec. 1–2)

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrability over authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism must rest on demonstrable grounds, not on the mere authority of celebrated names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advancing points of superiority in modern art, one must provide demonstrable evidence which can be met on its own grounds and not simply overborne by appeal to great names. (Sec. 4)

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish principles, not blanket labels for 'old masters'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not group different kinds of historical painters together under a single honorific term without analyzing their differing principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin warns against lumping fifteenth-century historical painters and seventeenth-century landscape painters both as 'old masters' — their principles and aims differ and must be judged separately. (Sec. 4)

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as the standard of all excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth (fidelity to nature/principle) is the proper standard by which excellence in art should be judged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout the work Ruskin treats 'truth' (literal and scientific fidelity in depiction) as the measure of artistic value. He aims to compare the 'truth' manifested by different artists across subjects. (CH III Sec.7 and general framing)

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty and qualifications of the critic/press
rubrics_metrics.description: The press and critics have a duty to advance art, and must possess proper qualifications to discharge it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should be informed by judgment and knowledge; the press should help the cause of art by exercising informed and consistent criticism rather than pandering to taste or fashion. (CH III Secs.10–11, 14)

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish works perfectly; beware cult of unfinished
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a necessity of finishing works of art perfectly; modern morbid fondness for unfinished works is objectionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin criticizes the contemporary fondness for unfinished works as self-defrauding and harmful to artists; both the duty to finish and appropriate encouragement of sketches should be balanced. (CH III Secs.15–19, 19–20)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tolerating mere brilliancy in young artists
rubrics_metrics.description: Brilliancy of execution or mere efforts at invention in young artists should not be tolerated at the expense of fundamental knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Young artists must be trained in fundamental truth and finish rather than encouraged in flashy tricks or immature invention. (CH III Sec.20)

rubrics_metrics.name: Observance of minor parts distinguishes master from novice
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful observance of minor parts and points (details) is the real distinction between masters and novices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small, well-observed particulars (ground, soil, rock detail, small foliar or geological features) are essential; their observance is a key test of artistic truth and maturity. (Foreg. CH Secs.14–16; Foreground CH Sec.29–30)

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of structural/geological truth in earth and hills
rubrics_metrics.description: The first laws of the earth's organization (structure of plains, mountains, beds, joints, lamination) are essential to truthful landscape depiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists must study the geological structure: plains as rest, hills as action; mountains supporting plains; beds and lamination in inferior mountains — all these details inform correct contour, slope, and character. (SECTION IV CH I & CH II–III)

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity governs apparent character of clouds and forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent differences in character between lower and central clouds (and between near and distant objects) depend chiefly on proximity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Near clouds differ in color and definiteness of form versus distant ones; painters must account for these effects when rendering sky and atmosphere. (CH IV Secs.1–4)

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and difficulty of painting rain-clouds and mist
rubrics_metrics.description: The rain-cloud and effects of mist are of high value to the painter but are difficult to render; old masters scarcely painted them, moderns (e.g., Turner) excel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rain-clouds present particular observational challenges; Turner and several moderns demonstrated superior power in rendering them, while older painters left few true examples. (CH IV Secs.5–7, 27–29)

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual character of parts and minute circumstance for tempest expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The individual character of parts and minute touches/circumstances convey the entire expression of tempest or other atmospheric states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner's expression of tempest is often given by small, decisive touches and contrasted passages (rest vs. agitation), requiring careful observation of detail and contrast. (CH IV Secs.17, 20–21)

rubrics_metrics.name: Water laws: imperfect reflective surface and inherent hue
rubrics_metrics.description: General laws of water: the reflective surface of water is imperfect; the inherent hue of water modifies dark reflections but not correct (right) ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical water-painting must account for how water's color and surface condition affect reflections; this differentiates faithful from merely plausible representations. (SECTION V CH I Secs.6–7)

rubrics_metrics.name: Water takes no shadow
rubrics_metrics.description: Water does not itself take a shadow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shadows modify the appearance of reflections and darker areas but water as a medium should not be treated as an object that 'takes' a shadow in the same way solid surfaces do; careful handling of shadow/reflection interplay is required. (SECTION V CH I Sec.8)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of ripple and motion on reflections
rubrics_metrics.description: Ripple and motion elongate and deflect reflections; moving water alters the appearance and arrangement of reflected images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists must understand how ripples, inclined surfaces, and agitation elongate, deflect, or obscure reflected images; treatment differs for horizontal vs inclined images and for calm vs agitated water. (SECTION V CH I Secs.11–15)

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of scientific observation and watchfulness; licenses/errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Painting water (and other phenomena) requires both scientific understanding and watchfulness; even great men take licenses which can be errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin cautions against complacent imitation of past masters' 'licenses' — errors in rendering reflections, movement, or color — and urges careful study and avoidance of unpardonable departures. (SECTION V CH I Sec.16–19)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection distinctness on distant water and texture of calm water
rubrics_metrics.description: All reflections on distant water are distinct; the texture of calm water requires special handling to avoid morbid clearness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner avoids over-distinct reflections in a way others do not; distant reflections appear crisp, but closer calm water has a subtle texture that must be painted to avoid unnatural sharpness. (SECTION V CH III Secs.5–11)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inexpressibility of certain sea effects; Turner's mastery of the open sea
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain effects (foam, shore-breakers) are essentially inexpressible in painting; yet Turner achieved noblest successes in depicting the deep open sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin notes formal limits (foam/shore-breakers cannot be truly represented) but praises Turner's 'Slave Ship' as an example of united excellences in sea-painting despite these difficulties. (SECTION V CH III Secs.29–39)

rubrics_metrics.name: Tree/bough laws: division, not taper; bough-drawing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Branches do not taper continuously but divide; boughs must diminish where they divide and multiply as they diminish; trees end in symmetrical curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate tree-drawing requires observing botanical laws: division patterns, repetition of buds, and natural concealment of parallelism. Many older painters violate these rules; moderns like Turner and J. D. Harding follow them more closely. (SECTION VI CH I Secs.2–5,9,25)

rubrics_metrics.name: Local color and foliage: variety, unity, and expressive 'green'
rubrics_metrics.description: Leafage has variety and symmetry; local color (green) must be rendered in a way expressive of light and not offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists should study leafage complexity and the expression of green to convey light appropriately; some painters show perfect unity in foliage while others fail. (SECTION VI CH I Secs.16–21,34)

rubrics_metrics.name: No man draws one thing well if he can draw nothing else
rubrics_metrics.description: Excellent artists exhibit fidelity across all subjects; versatility indicates genuine ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character and truth are manifested across different subjects; ability limited to a narrow set of mechanical tricks is insufficient evidence of true genius. (CH III Sec.5)

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor details tell the history of forms (rocks, soil, foreground)
rubrics_metrics.description: The geologic and compositional details of foreground elements (rocks, loose soil, detached blocks) tell the history of the scene and should be represented faithfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner's foregrounds reveal convex surfaces, fractured edges, and unified histories told by detail; faithful rendering of these minor parts contributes to art's truth. (Foreg. CH Secs.20–28; Foreground CH Secs.21–26)

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of precise terms and foundational principles for criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Introductory and foundational principles must be stated clearly because criticism is useless when its terms and grounds are ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin requests readers to attend to the introductory chapters setting the principles on which right judgment must be founded; technical jargon must be avoided or defined. (Introductory remarks after Sec.4)

rubrics_metrics.name: The critic's duty to confront established prejudice when warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: Those capable of demonstrating superiority in modern art must face opposition and challenge consecrated prejudices when warranted by demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due to the tyrannical influence of established reputation, critics with demonstrable points should not hesitate to oppose unjustified reverence for older or established works. (Sec.2–4)
